Regardless of ethical issues, which does not seem to be what you're asking, it's legal because Congress has the right to subcontract public services to private facilities, like the IRS and the USPS. Furthermore, the private company providing the service has a certain level of discretion on how to actually implement that service. That was the basis of the majority SCOTUS opinion on whether or not the IRS was correctly allowing tax breaks for health insurance exchanges. It was determined that despite the fact that congress boned up the law (because they rushed it through so no one could question it), the IRS had the right to determine how to best apply the law.

Whether or not this is a good idea is a separate conversation. There's a reason that the USPS simply can't compete with UPS, FedEx, or DHS (The delivery service, that is). The USPS knows that it doesn't have to compete to stay in business and that if they aren't making enough money, they can just hold up Congress for more by threatening to cut services. The IRS are a pack of right bastards because it's easier to be a dick than it is to put any effort into a case. And because there's no one else that provides that service.

Unfortunately, in this case there's a major problem. There is no civilian need for a prison system. The only institution that needs it is the government. This creates what economists call a "monopsony", which is the opposite of a monopoly. A monopsony occurs when there's only one consumer for a service- in this case, the government. Which means the consumer dictates how the service provider operates because the provider has no one else to provide the service to. And in this case, the sole customer doesn't care how the service is provided so long as no one has to publicly answer to it.
